text:
IMO Headquarters, London. File Image. Image Credit: Ship & Bunker.

Liberia/Argentina/Panama GFI paper emerging as frontrunner alternative to NZF

Saudi Arabia, Russia, GCC states, and US all signalling support or interest

Remaining NZF backers include EU, Norway, and Pacific Island States

Japan paper draws interest as possible middle ground

Intersessional proposed for September, MEPC 85 for November

Support for the IMO's Net-Zero Framework (NZF) appears to be fading this week at MEPC 84 in London, with delegates increasingly favouring the alternative GFI-based framework submitted by Liberia, Argentina, and Panama, Ship & Bunker understands.

The Liberia proposal differs most notably from the IMO NZF in that is has a revised Global Fuel Intensity (GFI) framework, where emissions targets are adjusted based on the demonstrated uptake of commercially viable low-carbon fuels, and scraps the creation of an IMO Fund in favour of flexibility measures such as credit trading, banking, and limited borrowing to support compliance.

The committee, which began meeting on April 27, spent much of Tuesday working through national positions on the GHG agenda item.

But this is not to say the NZF has been completely abandoned, and it is understood that Mexico, Brazil, Australia, Colombia, Switzerland, South Africa, and Malta are all reported to have all expressed support for it, either in its current form or with modifications.

Norway is understood to also prefer the NZF but has indicated it could work with a separate paper submitted by Japan.

The EU, with Cyprus holding the Council presidency, also came out in support of the NZF.

Pacific Island states, which have been among the most vocal champions of the NZF given their acute vulnerability to climate change, are understood to be still pressing hard for the original NZF framework to be preserved.

The Liberia Proposal

But against that, Saudi Arabia is understood to have called for the committee to proceed on the basis of the Liberia paper, cancel the resumption of the second extraordinary session (MEPC/ES.2), and instead convene an intersessional working group.

Ship & Bunker understands that any such intersessional working group on GHG would be scheduled for September, with MEPC 85 then taking place mid-November.

Russia and Sierra Leone have also backed the Liberia proposal, Ship & Bunker understands, and by late in the day GCC states were also said to be aligning broadly behind it.

The United States, which has formally submitted its opposition to the NZF (MEPC 84/7/41), reiterated its position and called for intersessional work to consider all alternative proposals.

Washington is understood to have described the Liberia paper as "interesting" - language that, while measured, amounts to a degree of endorsement from the party seen as most responsible for blocking the NZF at MEPC/ES.2 last October.

Singapore is reported to have indicated it is open to compromise and has expressed support for the Japan paper, while Turkey and Tanzania are also understood to be open to alternative proposals.

China has indicated openness to alternatives without backing any specific submission, sources told Ship & Bunker.

The EU, meanwhile, appears to be weighing its options as the prospect of an intersessional process grows - a move that would effectively defer and potentially reshape the NZF.

Japan's paper, which has drawn interest from Norway and Singapore as a possible middle ground, proposes keeping the NZF's GFI trajectory and surplus unit mechanism but removing mandatory payments into the IMO Net-Zero Fund - a key sticking point for many and the element some critics have likened to a global carbon tax.

It also calls for easing emissions targets from 2030 onwards, citing concerns that current levels could constrain the use of fuels such as LNG.

Tokyo has described the proposals as intended to bridge divisions and said it remains open to other ideas, positioning itself as a potential broker between the NZF bloc and those pushing for a more fundamental rewrite.

MEPC 84 runs until May 1.

First Port-to-Ship Ammonia Bunkering Achieved in Ulsan

The commercial shipping sector's shift toward ammonia fuel achieved a new milestone last week, according to The Maritime Executive. The Ulsan Port Authority in South Korea reported that the first port-to-ship bunkering of ammonia on an ocean-going vessel took place on April 23.

Lotte Fine Chemical, serving as the designated sustainable marine fuel supply demonstration operator, supplied roughly 600 tons of clean ammonia via the port-to-ship method at Pier 2 of Ulsan Main Port. The operation involved the gas tanker Antwerpen, built by HD Hyundai as the first in a series of vessels for Exmar.

Byun Jae-young, President of the Ulsan Port Authority, stated that the milestone was made possible by the port's advanced energy infrastructure and accumulated bunkering expertise, demonstrating the port's readiness to support various sustainable marine fuels. To facilitate this achievement, the port authority signed a Memorandum of Understanding in January 2024 to promote the ammonia bunkering industry, collaborating with stakeholders such as Korean Register, Lotte Fine Chemical, HD Hyundai Heavy Industries, and HMM across policy, infrastructure, vessel readiness, and fuel supply.

The 46,000 cubic meter gas carrier, ordered in 2023 and named earlier in April at the HD Hyundai shipyard, measures 190 meters in length. It was designed to transport liquefied gas cargoes including ammonia and LPG, and can also use its cargo, including ammonia, as fuel. The Antwerpen remains docked in Ulsan while its sister ship, Arlon, is completing sea trials and is scheduled for delivery to Exmar in June.

In preparation for the bunkering, Lotte Fine Chemical announced in March that it had completed the world's first commercial import of green ammonia, marking the first cross-border trade of that fuel. The green ammonia was produced entirely using renewable energy from wind and solar power at the world's largest green hydrogen and ammonia production complex, developed by Envision and located in Inner Mongolia, China. Lotte developed storage capabilities for the green ammonia at the Port of Ulsan and plans to use it for carbon-free energy applications, including ammonia marine bunkering, co-firing power generation, and as a hydrogen carrier.

Earlier ammonia bunkering demonstrations included a vessel operation in Singapore in early 2024 involving three tonnes of liquid ammonia loaded from Vopak's Banyan Terminal on Jurong Island, placed aboard Fortescue's converted offshore supply vessel. Two tugboats are currently the only other vessels capable of operating on ammonia, with Japan reporting ammonia bunkering from tank trucks to a tug converted from LNG to ammonia as part of an ongoing demonstration.

The American Biofuels Maritime Initiative (ABMI) has urged the U.S. government to take a leading role and highlight the role biofuels at the IMO, as it develops new global rules for shipping fuels.

In a letter to Secretary of State Marco Rubio, issues on 23 April, ABMI stresses that upcoming decisions by the 84th Marine Environment Protection Committee (MEPC 84, April 27 – 1 May) will shape the future of maritime energy, and that U.S. leadership is essential to ensure policies remain flexible and inclusive.

Specifically, they advocate for a “technology-neutral” framework that allows fuels like ethanol, biodiesel, renewable diesel, and bio-LNG to compete alongside other options.

ABMI argues that such an approach would support key U.S. interests by expanding export opportunities for American-made biofuels and aligning with broader trade goals.

They point to existing domestic policy, such as the Renewable Fuel Standard from the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), which sets strong targets for renewable fuel use, as evidence of the country’s production capacity and commitment to homegrown energy.

As the International Maritime Organization considers the future of maritime fuels, we appreciate the United States working to advance a technology-neutral approach that fully includes American-made biofuels. Expanding into maritime markets will drive new demand for U.S. farmers, support rural economies, and strengthen our nation’s position as a global energy leader

… said Geoff Cooper, President and CEO of the Renewable Fuels Association.

At the same time, the group highlights economic pressures facing U.S. biofuel producers and farmers, including limited demand, volatile crop prices, and financial losses.

As explained, if a cohesive international framework is not implemented in the near-term, restrictive, regional regulations like FuelEU Maritime, which effectively prohibits the use of American-made biofuels, will continue to unduly burden the international shipping market.

According to the initiative, opening maritime markets to biofuels could help relieve these pressures by creating new demand, boosting agricultural output, and strengthening rural economies.

This is one of the best opportunities the U.S. has had in recent memory to create new markets for American-made biofuels. Support by the Administration now will catalyze new investment, infrastructure, and projects that largely benefit American farms

… commented Patrick Serfass, Executive Director of the American Biogas Council.

Attacked by Trump

Members of the U.N. shipping body are gathering for talks this week in London to discuss a framework aimed at curbing carbon pollution from shipping.

President Donald Trump has personally assailed those efforts, and his administration’s sustained campaign against a tax forced the IMO to delay a vote on the measures last October.

The head of the U.S. delegation suggested last week that there was no hope for the so-called Net Zero Framework if and when it was brought up for a vote.

The Net Zero Framework calls for a carbon-intensity standard that would become stricter over time, encouraging industry to switch from fossil fuels to lower-emission alternatives. Ships that don’t meet the standard would need to pay a fee, which would then be used to help fund the shift to greener fuels and support developing countries.

The European Union, Kenya and other nations say they support the embattled measure and plan to defend them at this week’s talks.

‘Fundamental flaws’

The data being circulated through the halls of the IMO is at odds with prevailing analyses and ignores the benefits that would come from implementing the framework, experts said.

James Stewart, a research fellow in the data analytics of transport at the UCL Energy Institute, said he was able to reverse-engineer the U.S. methodology and had found “fundamental flaws” in how the flyers derived their estimates.

“Whilst there are a number of different issues with the approach taken, the most significant is in its overestimation of the contribution of fuel cost to total trade costs,” Stewart said, adding: “The error over-inflates compliance cost estimates and thereby overstates the NZF’s impact to a large extent.”

“This isn’t credible analysis, it’s a calculated exaggeration designed to scare members,” said Felix Klann, shipping policy officer at Transport & Environment. Klann said the IMO already provides robust data on transition costs and accused Washington of “bad-faith miscalculation and fearmongering to protect fossil fuel interests.”

Em Fenton, senior director of climate diplomacy at the NGO Opportunity Green, said the “renewed push from the U.S. to undermine a hard-fought multilateral agreement comes as no surprise.”

Alternatives to the Net Zero Framework proposed at the IMO meeting “offer insignificant climate benefits and are inherently unjust and inequitable,” they added.

The White House and U.S. State Department did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Senior representatives from ports, industry and policy institutions across the Baltic Sea Region gathered in Hamburg on April 23 for a workshop examining the energy transition and decarbonisation of transport, held at the HHLA Container Terminal Tollerort.

The event was organised by the Free and Hanseatic City of Hamburg’s Senate Chancellery Baltic Sea Strategy Point in cooperation with Port of Hamburg Marketing, with support from HHLA.

The workshop was framed around the strategic importance of ports as geopolitical assets and key enablers of Europe’s energy transition, with the specific objective of strengthening the visibility of port-related decarbonisation challenges within the EU Strategy for the Baltic Sea Region and fostering cross-sectoral collaboration across energy, transport, safety and shipping policy areas.

Participants identified long-term regulatory stability as a central prerequisite for driving decarbonisation and the energy transition at scale, alongside the need for stronger regional collaboration to share best practices, coordinate investments and develop replicable solutions.

The importance of sustained funding for pilot projects and continued efficiency improvements were also emphasised as enabling conditions for progress.

Discussion sessions addressed a broad range of topics including the current status of decarbonisation efforts at the Port of Hamburg, covering onshore power supply, alternative fuel infrastructure and green shipping corridor development.

Emerging marine fuels including methanol, ammonia and hydrogen were examined from a market perspective, alongside the role of hinterland rail connectivity in enabling sustainable logistics chains and the operational challenges facing the shipping industry in reducing emissions.

Digital coordination and cross-sector collaboration were highlighted as tools for unlocking further efficiency gains.

A key conclusion from the workshop was that sustainable port and logistics infrastructure is essential to building a resilient Baltic Sea Region, and that progress requires coordinated action across institutional, commercial and operational levels.

text:
European Union (EU) Ministers meeting in Lefkosia have endorsed the Lefkosia Declaration, placing people at the heart of maritime policy while committing to a competitive, sustainable and socially responsible future for European shipping.

The Declaration was signed during the informal Transport, Telecommunications and Energy Council meeting (Maritime Affairs), which took place on 29 April 2026 at the Filoxenia Conference Centre in Lefkosia, in the context of the Cyprus Presidency of the Council of the EU.

The Declaration places people at the centre of maritime policy. It focuses on strengthening seafarers’ education and training, re‑skilling and up‑skilling in view of the green and digital transitions, promoting seafaring and maritime professions and the equal participation of women in the maritime sector.

At a time of increased geopolitical challenges and rapid transformation, the ministerial meeting and the signature of the Lefkosia Declaration send a clear political message of unity and commitment: that European shipping can be competitive, sustainable and at the same time socially responsible.

“The Lefkosia Declaration represents a meaningful step towards a European maritime sector that is resilient, competitive, sustainable and socially responsible. Above all, it points towards a maritime sector that recognises its people as its most valuable asset.”

Marina Hadjimanolis, Shipping Deputy Minister of the Republic of Cyprus

During the Council meeting, the discussion focused on the Lefkosia Declaration on enhancing seafarers’ education and training, as well as promoting the equal participation of women in the shipping industry, which the Ministers signed after the exchange of views.

The Lefkosia Declaration reflects a shared political commitment to strengthening the human dimension of Europe’s maritime sector, recognising that Europe’s competitiveness, resilience and strategic autonomy ultimately depend on the skills, well-being and inclusiveness of its maritime workforce.

Throughout the discussion, EU Ministers had the opportunity to exchange views on key challenges and priorities related to maritime skills, training, working conditions and gender equality, sending a clear collective political message in support of a socially sustainable European maritime sector, ready to embrace the future.

On the sidelines of the Council, an award ceremony also took place for the winners of the European School Competition entitled “The Ship of the Future – My Ship in 60 years”, organised by the European Community Shipowners’ Associations.

See the relevant photos on the Cyprus Presidency’s Flickr account.

text:
What if a commercial tanker could run for years without taking on a single gallon of diesel, not because it found a miracle fuel, but because it brought its own power plant aboard?

That is the pitch behind a new collaboration between Scorpio Tankers and U.S. nuclear startup AMPERA, built around compact “micronuclear” reactors designed for ports, offshore sites, and eventually oceangoing ships.

The climate angle is hard to ignore. Shipping is under growing pressure to cut emissions while still moving nearly everything we buy, from everyday essentials to industrial equipment.

The big question now is whether nuclear microreactors can move from ambitious press releases to hardware that regulators, port authorities, insurers, and coastal communities are willing to live with.

Why the industry is looking beyond diesel

International shipping’s emissions have not been a rounding error. The International Maritime Organization says total shipping greenhouse gas emissions rose from 1.075 billion tons in 2012 to 1.183 billion tons in 2018, and shipping’s share of global anthropogenic emissions increased from 2.76% to 2.89% over the same period.

At the same time, the IMO’s 2023 strategy raises the bar. It calls for net-zero greenhouse gas emissions from international shipping “by or around” 2050, with checkpoints that aim to cut total annual emissions by at least 20% by 2030, striving for 30%, and at least 70% by 2040, striving for 80%, compared to 2008.

What the new reactor pitch looks like

Scorpio Tankers says it has entered a strategic collaboration with AMPERA to develop and commercialize advanced micronuclear power solutions for marine and shipping markets.

The company frames it as a response to demand for “reliable, zero-carbon power” in maritime, offshore, and port infrastructure, starting with floating nuclear power barges in the near term and nuclear-powered vessels over the longer term.

The business commitment is not small, even by big-shipping standards. Scorpio Tankers says its $10 million investment in AMPERA reflects its conviction that nuclear microreactors could change how ships and offshore infrastructure are powered, and the collaboration also mentions commercial models like power-as-a-service, leasing, and long-term service agreements.

On the technology side, the companies describe AMPERA’s system as compact and fully containerized, using thorium fuel in a subcritical, solid-state design that is “never refueled,” with proprietary 3D-printing manufacturing.

AMPERA’s own materials describe factory-built systems designed to deliver roughly 15 to 30 MWe, which is a scale that could matter for ports and certain offshore loads, even if full deep-sea propulsion is a different challenge.

Ports first, then open water

Starting at the dock is not an accident. Scorpio Tankers explicitly puts floating nuclear power barges first, alongside port and coastal power infrastructure, before moving to nuclear-powered commercial vessels over the longer term.

In practical terms, that means the earliest “marine nuclear” wins might look more like utility projects than futuristic ships. A barge supplying steady electricity can support port operations and offshore activity where power demand is high and diesel deliveries are expensive, and it can do it without the constant fuel logistics that drive up costs and emissions.

Indeed, nuclear at sea has a history. The U.S. Maritime Administration notes that the N.S. Savannah, launched in 1959, was the world’s first nuclear-powered merchant ship, built to promote the peaceful use of nuclear energy.

It proved the concept was possible, but it also showed how economics, regulation, and public acceptance can decide what “works” in the real world.

Regulators and security teams will ask hard questions

One reason this idea is resurfacing now is that regulation is shifting. The U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission says it has issued a new licensing pathway, known as Part 53, designed to make licensing advanced reactors faster and more predictable while maintaining safety, using technology-inclusive and risk-informed approaches with graded security requirements.

AMPERA is already positioning itself for that environment.

In a company announcement carried by PR Newswire, AMPERA said it submitted a letter to the NRC on Feb. 23, 2026 to begin the pre-application process for a factory-fabricated, containerized microreactor using advanced fuel forms and passive safety features, and it said it requested an initial pre-application meeting before the end of May.

Still, “can it be licensed” is only one slice of the problem. Deploying reactors for maritime use raises safeguards and security issues that go beyond a typical land-based installation, because nuclear material has to remain protected and accounted for throughout its life.

The IAEA notes that safeguards agreements exist to verify nuclear material is not diverted to weapons or other nuclear explosive devices, and any future maritime deployment model will have to fit that reality.

What to watch next

There is a straightforward reason shipping executives are listening. Scorpio Tankers and AMPERA argue micronuclear systems could cut fuel costs, reduce weight, improve efficiency, increase capacity, and eliminate carbon emissions for shipping companies, but the companies also flag that these plans are forward-looking and subject to risk and uncertainty.

In other words, nobody should treat “decades without refueling” as a delivery schedule.

For 2026, the near-term signals are more procedural than flashy. Watch whether AMPERA’s NRC engagement advances beyond pre-application steps, whether Scorpio and AMPERA can define realistic port-focused deployments, and how insurers and port authorities react once there is a concrete proposal on paper instead of a concept.

That is when the idea will either gain traction, or hit the wall.

text:
Venture Energy Limited and Shanghai Shenji Energy & Environmental Technology Co Ltd announced the signing of a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU), upgrading their existing spot trade relationship into a broader, full-spectrum partnership focusing on green fuels.

The agreement expands cooperation beyond spot trading to include medium- and long-term offtake arrangements, green fuel trial bunkering, development of trading platforms and technical management services for marine vessels. As stated, the MoU was signed on 17 April 2026 at the headquarters of Shenergy Group in Shanghai by Greg McMillan, executive director of Venture Energy, and Zhu Jiaqi, chairman of Shenergy Environmental Technology Co., Ltd.

Under the agreement, Venture Energy and Shenji Energy establish a hybrid supply framework that combines spot market flexibility with long-term offtake commitments. This structure is designed to provide more stable and predictable access to green marine fuels amid rising global demand for regulatory-compliant low-carbon energy.

Venture Energy has already signaled its intent to scale up procurement volumes starting this year.

Furthermore, the partnership also extends beyond fuel supply into integrated maritime services, with a focus on three key areas:

development of a green fuel trading platform

pilot bunkering operations and market expansion for green fuels

collaboration on marine services and ship management.

Together, these initiatives aim to strengthen coordination across the value chain and support the wider adoption of green fuels in global shipping markets.

Greg McMillan, Executive Director of Venture Energy, stated: “This strategic collaboration marks an important milestone in Venture Energy’s green fuel supply chain development. Through our partnership with Shenji Energy, we are able to secure a stable supply of green methanol while also establishing an early position across other green fuel pathways. Together, this enables us to offer more comprehensive decarbonization solutions to shipping customers worldwide.”

The move comes at a pivotal moment in the global maritime energy transition. Regulatory pressure from the EU is accelerating the adoption of cleaner fuels across the shipping sector and other industries, with similar momentum expected from forthcoming IMO regulations.

He further notes that decarbonisation requires a level playing field, robust enforcement, and alignment across regions. In this context, the WSC maintains a long-term approach to climate policy, supporting industry compliance while keeping sight of the broader strategic picture.

SAFETY4SEA: Congratulations on your new role at the World Shipping Council. What motivated you to take on this position, and what are your key priorities?

Simon Bergulf: I’ve spent more than two decades in maritime, and decarbonisation has been a constant thread throughout that time. The scale of the transition the industry is now facing makes this a particularly important moment to step into this role. What motivated me is being able to work within an organisation with such exceptional depth of knowledge and expertise. Beyond that it was the opportunity to help shape how that transition is delivered, working closely with governments and industry to turn ambition into reality at global scale, is challenging but hugely exciting.

S4S: This is a critical time for the maritime industry. What concerns you most today regarding the industry’s transformation and why?

S.B.: It has become very clear that a global and stable regulatory framework is imperative to secure the industry’s transition. The industry has already made significant investments, but without a clear, coordinated global framework, there is a risk those efforts don’t deliver at scale. Ensuring a level playing field, strong enforcement and alignment across regions is essential to keeping the transition on track. I believe WSC has a duty of keeping a long-term approach on climate policy: helping the industry navigate immediate regulatory choices without losing sight of the ultimate objective. That also means bringing the commercial dimension into the discussion, including investment realities both in CAPEX and OPEX terms.

S4S: With upcoming IMO discussions on decarbonization and green fuels, what role will WSC play under your leadership to ensure the industry’s voice is effectively represented?

S.B.: WSC’s role is to bring a clear, unified industry perspective to the table. As reflected in the recent joint industry statement, there is strong alignment across shipping in support of a global measure at the IMO to decarbonise shipping, and the need to move forward without delay. We will continue to engage constructively with governments, highlighting both the investment industry has already made to prepare for the transition and the practical conditions needed to scale lower emission fuels.

S4S: Green fuels and new ship designs are essential to decarbonization. How do you view the pace of technological innovation compared to the regulatory frameworks needed to support it?

S.B.: More than 400 dual-fuel container ships and vehicle carriers are already on the water, with over 700 more on order, showing that the transition is well underway. That reflects more than $150 billion in industry investment to prepare the fleet for cleaner fuels. In many ways, industry investment is moving ahead of the framework however, we won’t realise the emissions reductions without it. A clear global framework is needed to support fuel production, infrastructure and investment certainty, so the progress already being made can translate into real emissions reductions.

text:
Deendayal Port Authority (DPA) has signed a memorandum of understanding with the International Council on Clean Transportation (ICCT) to develop strategies aimed at reducing greenhouse gas and air pollution emissions from port and shipping operations at Kandla in Gujarat.

The agreement, signed in New Delhi on Wednesday, will centre on research, policy development and knowledge-sharing to support low-emission shipping practices, combining ICCT’s technical expertise with DPA’s operational experience.

Advt

Under the collaboration, the two sides will identify high-impact decarbonisation measures across ships, fuels, port-linked transport and in-port equipment, while assessing the infrastructure and regulatory changes needed to implement them at scale. The exercise will aim to produce actionable recommendations for deployment.

Broader scope across port ecosystem

The partnership will examine emissions reduction pathways across the wider port ecosystem, including maritime operations, cargo handling and hinterland transport such as trucking. It will also assess enabling conditions such as infrastructure readiness and institutional capacity, along with policy and market mechanisms required to support low- and zero-emission solutions.

Amit Bhatt, India managing director at ICCT, said, “Through this partnership with Deendayal Port Authority, we will identify practical, high-impact solutions, from cleaner marine fuels to electric trucks and zero-emission port equipment that can substantially reduce emissions while enhancing operational efficiency.”

DPA chairman Sushil Kumar Singh said the collaboration would help accelerate the port’s transition. “Our partnership with ICCT will help accelerate Deendayal Port’s transition into a future-ready, green port by combining our operational expertise with ICCT’s global technical knowledge,” he said.

Push for greener ports

The agreement comes amid increasing focus on decarbonising maritime transport and port infrastructure. ICCT works with regulators on transport emissions, while DPA plays a key role in India’s maritime trade and is pursuing measures to improve sustainability and efficiency.

text:
Russia tabled a last-minute proposal on the opening day of MEPC 84, seeking changes to Paragraph 12 of Regulation 27 under MARPOL Annex VI.

Regulation 27 requires ships of 5,000 gross tonnage and above to collect and report fuel oil consumption data to the IMO Ship Fuel Oil Consumption Database.

Paragraph 12 of this regulation states that “The Secretary-General of the Organization shall maintain an anonymized database such that identification of a specific ship will not be possible. Parties shall have access to the anonymized data strictly for their analysis and consideration.”

Russia proposed either deleting the paragraph entirely or amending it so that anonymised data could only be shared with other states with “the consent of the relevant flag state.”

The proposal was backed by several petrostates, including Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Iran and Iraq, as well as India, Thailand, Nigeria and Ghana.

The EU bloc, including Cyprus, Greece, Malta and France, alongside Brazil, opposed the proposal and called for the existing text to remain unchanged.

The Marshall Islands, Cook Islands and Denmark said they were unable to take a position on the proposal due to the timing of the submission.

MEPC Chair Harry T. Conway said changes could not be made through an informal floor intervention and would need to follow the IMO’s formal submission and decision-making procedures.

text:
Green or e-ammonia produced entirely with renewable energy has emerged as an alternative marine fuel for decarbonizing global shipping due to its carbon-free composition, compatibility with combustion engines and fuel cells, and relatively low production cost1,2,3,4. Interest in e-ammonia has grown following the International Maritime Organization’s (IMO) 2023 Greenhouse Gas (GHG) Strategy to reach net-zero GHG emissions by mid-century5. On a lifecycle basis, e-ammonia can have up to ~80% lower direct GHG emissions than conventional marine fuels, such as very-low-sulfur fuel oil (VLSFO), the current dominant marine fuel6,7.

Unlike VLSFO, the impacts of which are dominated by carbon dioxide (CO2) and other conventional fossil fuel-derived emissions, including methane, volatile organic compounds, nitrogen oxides (NOx), and sulfur oxides (SOx), e-ammonia’s impacts are driven to a larger extent by reactive nitrogen (Nr) emissions—nitrous oxide (N2O), ammonia (NH3), and NOx—which pose distinct environmental concerns8,9. N2O is a potent GHG, with ~273 times the global warming potential (GWP) of CO2 over 100 years, and is also an ozone-depleting substance10. NH3 and NOx are short-lived air pollutants that contribute to the formation of fine particulate matter (PM2.5)—especially when co-emitted—and lead to associated health impacts10. Crucially, Nr species also undergo sequential chemical and biological transformations within the nitrogen cycle, leading to multiple environmental impacts11. Atmospheric NH3 and NOx are deposited to land and water bodies, increasing Nr loading in ecosystems—primarily as ammonium (NH4+) formed from NH3, and nitrate (NO3–) produced from NOx and NH4+10,11. This excess Nr drives eutrophication—characterized by excessive algal growth, increased organic matter decomposition, and oxygen depletion—which can reduce species diversity and alter ecosystem functioning10,11. Additionally, NH3 can contribute to N2O formation (i.e., indirect N2O) via atmospheric reactions12, and deposition of both NH3 and NOx can further promote indirect N2O production, reinforcing climate impacts13. NOx also participates in photochemical reactions that produce ground-level ozone10.

Nr losses occur across the ammonia marine fuel (AMF) value chain—from production and distribution to storage, bunkering (i.e., vessel refueling), and use (Supplementary Fig. 1). NH3 combustion produces NOx and N2O, while incomplete combustion results in unburned NH3 (“ammonia slip”)6. Moreover, direct NH3 losses can occur throughout the value chain via unintentional leakage (e.g., fugitive leaks, accidental spills) and operational releases such as boil-off gas (BOG) and flaring7,8,14. Without stringent mitigation measures (e.g., gas recapture and leak detection <10 ppm), the Nr waste could be substantial, i.e., large enough to affect climate, local air quality, and nitrogen deposition at emission sites15,16.

Current global Nr inputs ( ~ 210 Tg N/yr) far exceed the planetary nitrogen boundary—which represents the maximum safe budget of anthropogenic nitrogen fixation (62–82 Tg N/yr), i.e., the conversion of inert atmospheric nitrogen into Nr17—largely due to synthetic ammonia-based fertilizer use ( ~ 112 Tg N/yr), livestock manure, and fossil fuel combustion17,18. Only a part of this large Nr input is taken up by plants and microbes; the rest leaks into ecosystems, driving environmental degradation19. In agriculture, in particular, inefficient practices result in substantial Nr losses, contributing to water pollution and biodiversity loss, and climate warming through rising N2O emissions18,19. To better capture these losses, a global agricultural nitrogen surplus boundary ( ~ 43–57 Tg N/yr) has been proposed, representing the safe operating budget for Nr losses (safe global Nr surplus budget)19.

In the absence of sector-specific metrics, the safe global Nr surplus budget serves as a quantitative global benchmark for assessing additional anthropogenic pressures on the nitrogen cycle—highlighting that any new large-scale Nr source would intensify environmental risks in an already transgressed Earth system, with local impacts shaped by regional chemistry, microbiology, and where emissions occur20,21. Total global NH3 demand (all uses) is projected to rise from ~185 Tg/yr today—primarily for fertilizer production—to over 555 Tg/yr by 205022, with shipping (AMF) accounting for ~2.3 Tg in 2030, ~62 Tg in 2040, and ~245 Tg in 20503,23. Even relatively small Nr losses from the AMF value chain could, thus, add significantly to global Nr pollution, further straining the planetary nitrogen boundary and potentially offsetting international efforts to reduce agricultural NH3 emissions24. These risks must also be considered in relation to continued fossil fuel use in shipping, which currently contributes substantially to Nr pollution, primarily through NOₓ emissions25.

Wolfram et al. first noted that large-scale NH3 use in shipping could disrupt the global nitrogen cycle, underscoring the need for tighter controls and further research8. However, no study has yet quantified global Nr emissions across the full AMF value chain. Here, we estimate NH3, NOx, and N2O emissions from global AMF deployment under projected demand scenarios for 2030, 2040, and 20503. These first-order estimates span low- to high-emission scenarios, based on assumptions about leakage, BOG, and combustion emissions (Supplementary Table 1)7.

Our results indicate that under a low-emission scenario, AMF could substantially reduce value-chain Nr emissions relative to today’s VLSFO use, whereas under medium‑ and high‑emission scenarios, Nr losses could approach or exceed those from VLSFO. At the global scale, projected AMF deployment could account for ~2–21% of the global agricultural nitrogen surplus boundary by mid-century, with additional pressure on this already exceeded boundary determined by the effectiveness of emissions mitigation. At the same time, because emissions are concentrated in ports and along shipping lanes, even moderate increases may create exposure and deposition hotspots. Impacts will thus depend not only on total Nr losses but also on their spatial distribution and chemical form: elevated NH3 and NOx near coastal regions can worsen air pollution and increase nitrogen deposition to already overburdened ecosystems. Overall, our findings show that AMF can either reduce or amplify Nr pressures—depending on leakage across the value chain and on engine emissions—underscoring the need for strong prevention, regulation, and governance of Nr emissions in a defossilizing energy system.

Projected Nr emissions from the AMF value chain under low- to high-emission scenarios

Results (presented throughout as a minimum to maximum range) show that Nr emissions across the AMF value chain could represent ~0.5–4.4% of the nitrogen supplied in mass—~0.1–1.2% as NH3-N, ~0.4–2.9% as NOx-N, and ~0.01–0.3% as N2O-N (Supplementary Tables 2-4). On an energy basis (per unit energy delivered), this corresponds to 0.2–1.9 g N/MJ, potentially exceeding those from VLSFO (0.68 g N/MJ) by up to 185% (i.e., 2.85x), depending on the emissions scenario (Supplementary Fig. 2).

By 2040, AMF is projected to meet ~10% of shipping’s energy demand (assuming similar demand as today), resulting in Nr emissions of 0.3–2.2 Tg N/yr (Fig. 1A). Comparatively, VLSFO currently supplies over half of the sector’s energy26 and emits ~4.6 Tg N/yr. Although AMF would deliver only ~17% of the energy currently supplied by VLSFO, its Nr emissions could range from 6% to nearly 50% of those from VLSFO today—representing ~1–5% of the global agricultural nitrogen surplus boundary (i.e., safe global Nr surplus budget).

By 2050, AMF is projected to meet ~38% of shipping’s energy demand, resulting in Nr emissions of 1.0–8.8 Tg N/yr—equivalent to ~23 up to 192% of today’s VLSFO Nr emissions, despite AMF meeting only ~67% of the energy provided by VLSFO (Fig. 1A). NH3 emissions (0.2–2.4 Tg N/yr) could match or exceed global industrial NH3-N emissions ( ~ 1.6 g NH3-N/yr)27 in medium- and high-emissions scenarios (Fig. 1B and Supplementary Table 2). In total, AMF Nr emissions could represent ~2–21% of the global nitrogen surplus budget, with the upper estimate more than double Germany’s current total Nr emissions ( ~ 4 Tg N/yr)28.

Together, these results indicate that, without stringent mitigation, large-scale AMF deployment could become an important additional source of Nr pollution, surpassing current Nr emissions from VLSFO even while providing less energy. Supplementary Fig. 3 presents a hypothetical full-displacement comparison of AMF vs. VLSFO, each supplying 100% of the fleet’s current energy demand.

Ammonia emissions from representative bunkering operations

An important distinction between AMF and VLSFO use is the introduction of new NH3 emissions sources across the value chain. AMF production, bunkering, and combustion are potential major contributors to NH3 emissions (Fig. 1C–E and Supplementary Table 2). While production and combustion emissions are under active investigation4,14, bunkering emissions remain poorly characterized. Because AMF has half the energy density of VLSFO, larger transfer volumes are required, increasing emission risks. To further estimate bunkering emissions, we modeled a representative bunkering operation using real-world and simulated AMF transfer rates and scaled it to global AMF demand (“Methods”). Results show that total NH3 emissions from bunkering operations—including leakage and BOG—could account for 0.04–0.07% of the transferred fuel (Supplementary Table 5), totaling ~0.02–0.03 Tg NH3-N/yr by 2040 and ~0.07–0.13 Tg NH3-N/yr by 2050. BOG contributes 24–44% of those emissions (Fig. 2A, B and Supplementary Table 5). These estimates are reported separately for operational context and are not added to the literature-based value‑chain totals in Fig. 1 (derived from Supplementary Table 1).

Implications of bunkering emissions for exposure and mitigation thresholds

To assess the potential health implications of NH3 exposure during bunkering, we applied a measurement-informed model to estimate global NH3 emissions from bunkering based on NH3 concentrations measured by sensors near the transfer system (“Methods”). Global emissions above 0.02 Tg NH3-N/yr in 2040 and 0.07 Tg NH3-N/yr in 2050 would correspond to universal sensor readings consistently in the hundreds of ppm within 2 m of the transfer system (Fig. 2C and Supplementary Table 6), far exceeding recommended short- and long-term exposure limits ( > 25 ppm and >10 ppm, respectively) and posing health risks29. Achieving near-zero bunkering emissions ( < 0.001 Tg NH3-N/yr) requires sensor readings consistently <2 ppm near transfer systems (Fig. 2D and Supplementary Table 6) and, consequently, in the ppb range farther away in open air.

Overall, our results indicate that at the lower end of current estimates, e-ammonia could reduce lifecycle Nr emissions per unit energy by ~66% compared to VLSFO; however, without mitigation, Nr emissions could nearly triple, exacerbating the existing Nr overshoot from fossil fuels and agriculture. By 2050, this range implies climate forcing from direct N2O ( ~ 8–224 Tg CO2-equivalents), alongside additional climate forcing (via indirect N2O formation), air-quality impacts, and deposition-driven ecosystem pressures from ~0.2–2.4 Tg NH3-N and ~0.8–5.8 Tg NOx-N. The wide range in outcomes reflects scenario bounds driven by uncertainty in the stage-specific emission rates applied across the AMF value chain (Supplementary Table 1), where the “low” and “high” values represent lower and upper literature-derived bounds, respectively. The spread is driven by (i) upstream NH3 leakage assumptions—particularly at production, where inventory-based estimates may underreport emissions by a factor of ~508,14,30—and (ii) combustion-stage Nr emission factors that vary across engine configurations and performance4,31,32,33,34,35. BOG emissions during storage and bunkering provide additional variability and are especially relevant for localized port impacts.

Further empirical data are needed to refine our Nr emission estimates, particularly measurements of NH3 leakage across the value chain, BOG emissions during storage and bunkering, and NH3, NOx, and N2O emissions from marine engines reported as mass- or energy-normalized emission factors (e.g., g Nr/kg-fuel or g Nr/MJ) across representative operating profiles. Such data would support the design of effective mitigation strategies as AMF deployment expands.

Our findings build on recent work examining the implications of AMF use for the global nitrogen cycle. Wolfram et al. highlighted the risk that ammonia‑based energy systems could disrupt nitrogen cycling as deployment scales8; our analysis addresses this concern by providing first‑order estimates of NH3, NOx, and N2O emissions across the AMF value chain (Supplementary Tables 2–4) and benchmarking them against existing fossil fuels (Fig. 1). Bertagni et al. similarly showed that the sustainability of an emerging NH3 economy depends critically on nitrogen loss rates across production, transport, and use14, and we extend this system‑level perspective by quantifying how these losses translate into Nr pressures under realistic fuel‑demand scenarios ( ~ 2–21% of the safe global Nr budget). Recent work by Wong et al. has advanced understanding of combustion‑stage emissions and their air‑quality impacts36; our results complement these insights by situating combustion emissions within a broader value‑chain context (Fig. 1) and by translating NH3 emissions from bunkering into representative sensor-based concentration thresholds relevant for protecting human health and the environment (i.e., <2 ppm; Fig. 2D). Together, these studies indicate that realizing the climate benefits of ammonia as a fuel requires coordinated control of Nr emissions across technologies, infrastructure, and governance scales.

Unmanaged AMF-related Nr emissions could undermine progress toward shipping’s net‑zero trajectory under the IMO’s 2023 GHG Strategy and run counter to the United Nations Environmental Assembly’s (UNEA) calls to accelerate action to significantly reduce nitrogen waste globally by 20305,37. Effective mitigation of Nr emissions is therefore essential to avoid trading carbon reductions for new Nr pressures. Based on our analysis, key measures include installing NH3 sensors within 2 m of likely emission points (e.g., valves, joints, seals, pipework, compression equipment) for rapid leak detection and repair, conducting routine scans to identify leaks as infrastructure scales, and implementing BOG capture and targeted leak prevention and control strategies (e.g., exhaust treatment technologies). These measures would help shift outcomes toward the low-emissions end of the modeled range.

While AMF-related Nr waste can be >90% lower than that from nitrogen-based fertilizer use (110 Tg N/yr)9, emissions will concentrate near ports and shipping lanes. Without effective mitigation, these localized emissions may increase coastal and marine nitrogen loading and create new, or exacerbate existing, nitrogen exposure inequities18,19. For instance, as short-lived air pollutants, NH3 and NOx emissions near ports and along shipping corridors can negatively impact public health10. Air pollutant emissions from conventionally-fueled ships currently contribute substantially to the global air pollution burden, particularly in port and coastal communities38,39, and the comparative public health impacts of AMF will depend heavily on the efficacy of NH3 and NOx emission controls36. Because AMF emissions differ in distribution and chemical form from Nr emissions from agriculture and conventionally-fueled ships, context-specific assessments will be crucial for addressing the impacts of AMF use and ensuring these do not deepen environmental and social inequities.

At the same time, it is important to highlight that, under the low-emission scenario, Nr emissions from AMF are notably lower than those from VLSFO. Currently, Nr emissions from shipping cause negative public health impacts, as outlined above38,39, as well as environmental effects, including eutrophication and acidification40,41. The lower emissions scenario modeled here highlights that, under the right conditions, transitioning from VLSFO to AMF can not only contribute to reducing shipping’s climate impact but can also reduce pressures on public health, the environment, and biodiversity. These interlinked opportunities highlight the imperative to minimize AMF-related Nr emissions.

An effectively designed policy is key for managing Nr emissions from the AMF value chain. To this end, a range of policy levers could be adapted or introduced. For example, shipping’s GHG emissions are priced under the European Union’s (EU) Emissions Trading System (ETS)42 and are the subject of measures being considered as part of the proposed IMO Net Zero Framework43. However, of the relevant Nr species, these measures target only direct N2O, while for AMF, NH3 and NOx emissions also contribute to climate impact through indirect N2O7. Adapting policies and regulations aimed at accelerating GHG-reductions—such as regional ETS as deployed in the EU and UK42,44, or potential future global instruments like the IMO Net Zero Framework43—to also tackle indirect N2O could help address the full range of Nr emissions arising from AMF use. Additionally, air pollution and environmental policies, regulations, and operational measures could be leveraged to control NH3 and NOx, which dominate AMF’s Nr emissions ( ~ 23–28% and ~66–75%, respectively). For instance, existing measures such as Emission Control Areas (ECAs)45—areas of the ocean in which restrictions aim to limit emissions of substances including NOx and SOx—and technical standards like the NOx Technical Code46—which sets out NOx emission standards for ship engines—could be used as a basis for future regulation of AMF’s NH3 and NOx emissions. Similarly, recent work has highlighted that controls on the discharge of NH3 effluents from ships to the marine environment could be required to minimize aqueous Nr inputs and their environmental impacts47. The stringency, geographic scope, and enforcement of such measures would likely be important determinants of their efficacy36.

Overall, effective mitigation of Nr emissions will require coordinated action across governance levels and sectors, particularly between maritime transport and agriculture. As NH3, NOx, and N2O contribute to climate warming, ecosystem degradation, and health impacts11, minimizing Nr emissions across the value chain is critical. With appropriate measures, widespread adoption of AMF can reduce fossil fuel emissions while maximizing climate benefits and minimizing the impact on the global nitrogen cycle.

Current shipping fuel demand

DNV estimates global marine fuel consumption at 300 Tg of oil, which corresponds to ~650 Tg of ammonia on an energy basis when converted using lower heating values (LHVs)3. VLSFO currently accounts for approximately 55% of total marine oil demand26.

Value-chain Nr emissions inventory

We estimated potential direct, operational NH3, NOx, and N2O emissions from the AMF value chain—covering production, distribution, liquefaction, in-port storage (1 day), bunkering, onboard storage (1 day), and combustion in the engine—under three global demand scenarios for 2030 (2.3 Tg), 2040 (62 Tg), and 2050 (245 Tg), based on projections from DNV3. These projections are used by the IMO in its Future Fuels and Technology Project (https://futurefuels.imo.org/), making them a policy-relevant baseline for fuel uptake trajectories. We present 2030/2040/2050 as illustrative deployment snapshots; emissions scale proportionally with assumed AMF demand. The IMO’s 2023 GHG Strategy includes emissions reduction targets for 2030/2040/2050, underscoring the relevance of these time points5. Higher-end projections suggest that AMF could account for 44% of shipping’s total energy demand by 2050 ( ~ 286 Tg), implying greater fuel use and associated Nr emissions than those estimated under the DNV-based scenario1.

To estimate NH3 emissions, we applied stage-specific emissions rates for leakage—including fugitive emissions and minor spills—and BOG across three scenarios representing low (L), medium (M), and high (H) levels of Nr loss (Supplementary Table 1). In this scenario framework, low rates reflect effective prevention and control across the value chain, whereas high rates reflect limited or absent controls; the medium case provides an intermediate scenario for comparison. Emission rates were compiled from Esquivel-Elizondo et al., and the primary sources cited therein7. The derivation, justification, and references for each stage and scenario bound (L/M/H) are provided in the Supplementary Methods (“Derivation and literature basis for Supplementary Table 1 emission rates”)7. Rates reflect literature-derived ranges and are intended for first-order scenario analysis; they should be refined as additional empirical data (e.g., measurements) become available. For each year (2030/2040/2050), we estimated annual NH3 emissions by multiplying the stage-specific emission rates (Supplementary Table 1) by the corresponding projected global AMF demand and summing across stages. Because BOG emission rates for storage are expressed on a per‑day basis, estimated storage‑stage emissions can be scaled by multiplying the daily rate by the assumed number of storage days. This scenario-based value-chain inventory is not a full life-cycle assessment and excludes upstream/background Nr emissions (e.g., from electricity generation and infrastructure).

We estimated NOx and N2O emissions for the combustion stage only; for upstream stages, we focus on direct, on-site Nr releases (e.g., NH3 leakage and BOG). We converted ammonia demand to energy using its LHV of 18.6 MJ/kg6 and applied combustion emission rates (g Nr/MJ) summarized in Supplementary Table 17.

For comparison, we estimated value-chain NOx and N2O emissions from current VLSFO use by converting VLSFO demand to energy using an LHV of 41.2 MJ/kg and applying combustion emissions rates of 2 g NOx/MJ and 0.00278 g N2O/MJ from Schmidt et al.6. This energy‑basis comparison implicitly normalizes for engine efficiency and does not require assumptions about differences in propulsion efficiency between fuels. To approximate total value-chain emissions, we assumed combustion accounts for 90% of total Nr emissions, with upstream processes contributing the remaining 10%, consistent with findings from lifecycle assessments of fossil and alternative fuels6,48.

NH3 emissions from representative bunkering operations

Independent of the value-chain emissions inventory above, we modeled a representative bunkering operation to estimate bunkering-specific NH3 emissions under plausible conditions and demand scenarios. In this operational scenario, total bunkering emissions are calculated by combining process‑based BOG estimates with assumed ranges of fugitive leakage; these bunkering-specific estimates are reported only for Fig. 2A, B and are not incorporated into the value-chain totals in Fig. 1 (derived from Supplementary Table 1).

We calculated BOG emissions per bunkering operation using previously described methods and equations from Al-Breiki et al.2,16, assuming a pipe length of 10–20 m, no BOG recapture (i.e., full venting), and an average consumption of 4000 MJ/nautical mile (Supplementary File 1). We modeled a representative bunkering operation using an 8000 m3 fuel tank and a transfer volume of 7600 m3, based on a liquid ammonia density of 681.9 kg/m3 (refs. 6,29). To estimate transfer duration, we applied both real-world and simulated ammonia transfer rates ranging from 320 to 1086 m3/h49,50. We then scaled BOG emissions per operation by the number of bunkering events required to meet projected global AMF demand (from DNV)3. The number of bunkering events was calculated by dividing annual AMF demand by the AMF volume transferred per representative bunkering operation and multiplying by the annual number of trips per ship, as derived from the voyage duration assumptions (15-knot average speed; Supplementary File 1). This approach provides a first-order estimate of BOG-related NH3 emissions under plausible operational conditions and demand scenarios. The calculated BOG emission rates ( ~ 0.0156%) fall between the low- and medium-emission scenarios in Supplementary Table 1.

Fugitive NH3 emissions in this bunkering scenario were estimated similarly to those in the value-chain inventory—by applying a range of leakage rates (0.016–0.052% of fuel throughput) to the transferred ammonia volume (Supplementary Methods & Supplementary Table 1). Together, BOG and leakage emissions were summed to estimate total NH3 emissions per representative bunkering operation, which were then scaled to global ammonia demand scenarios for 2030, 2040, and 2050.

Measurement-informed sensor-based estimation of bunkering emissions

As a complementary, measurement-informed approach, we developed a mass flux model (Eq. 1) that translates consistent (i.e., sustained over a representative bunkering operation) NH3 concentrations near the transfer system into implied bunkering emission fluxes—without distinguishing between leakage and BOG. This framework does not use data from an operational bunkering site; rather, it assumes hypothetical but representative NH3 concentrations that could be detected by sensors located near the transfer system during bunkering.

$${{Mass}}\;{{emission}}\;{{rate}}\left(\frac{g}{s}\right)=\frac{\left[N{H}_{3}\right]* U* A* {M}_{{{NH}}3}}{{V}_{{{ideal}}}}$$

(1)

Where [NH3] is the ammonia concentration reported by the sensor in parts per million by volume (ppmv), converted to mol/mol by dividing by 1,000,000; U is the wind speed (6 m/s, typical of the Port of Rotterdam);2424 A is the cross-sectional area of the plume (4 m high by 10 m wide = 40 m2 in our model); MNH3 is ammonia’s molar mass (17.03 g/mol); and Videal is the molar volume of an ideal gas at conditions (24.45 L/mol or 0.02445 m3/mol at 25 °C and 1 atm).

This equation assumes that a consistent NH3 concentration measured within ~2 m of the transfer pipe represents the average NH3 concentration within a plume of air moving at a defined wind speed across a fixed area (A). In our model, A is a conservative estimate for the region immediately surrounding the transfer pipe or system. We normalized instantaneous NH3 mass emission rates (g/s) from Eq. 1 by ammonia transfer rates (320–1086 m3/h)49,50 to yield emission factors (g/m3). We then multiplied these factors by the assumed bunkered volume (7600 m3) to estimate NH3 emissions from a bunkering operation. Finally, we scaled these emissions by the number of bunkering operations required to meet the annual global ammonia demand (Supplementary File 1). This measurement-informed framework provides a means of interpreting NH3 concentrations (ppm) in terms of emissions magnitude (Tg NH3-N/yr) and identifying concentration thresholds relevant for protecting human health and the environment (e.g., <2 ppm; Fig. 2C, D and Supplementary Table 6).

Emission units

All emissions are expressed as nitrogen (i.e., NH3-N, NOx-N, and N2O-N) to enable comparison across Nr forms and against other anthropogenic sources.

To estimate the climate impact of direct N2O emissions from the AMF value chain, we converted N2O mass to CO2-equivalents using a 100-year Global Warming Potential (GWP) of 2739.

text:
LNG advocates SEA-LNG has reiterated its support for a single global regulatory framework as discussions continue at the MEPC 84 meeting this week at the IMO headquarters in London.

The discussions are complex, with delegates working to bridge differing positions on technical and economic issues in a difficult geopolitical environment, Steve Esau, COO at SEA-LNG, said in a statement on its website on Monday.

The coalition warned that regional fragmentation risks creating duplicated compliance costs, adding that such an outcome would serve neither the shipping industry nor broader climate goals.

“Our position remains clear: there can only be one global decarbonisation framework for maritime, Esau said.

“Regional fragmentation, with its risk of multiple and duplicated compliance costs, serves neither shipping nor the climate.

“We are calling for a framework that is goal-based and technology-neutral, that protects first movers, and that incentivises solutions which are practical, scalable and investable.”

Despite varied positions among member states, the organisation said it remains optimistic that common ground can be found.

It added that it will continue to support the process at the IMO, including contributing evidence on methane-based pathways.
